student did not watch all the lectures and practical videos necessary to achieve a higher performance and it was mandatory to watch each of them before submitting the assignment so the progress component presents this information as progress circles along with a percentage to show the student their current situation however which videos should be watched and the order are not shown in the progress component hence we introduced 3 a recommendation component that adds a recommendation box under each progress circle to inform the student about the list of essential items and their priority level to perform to achieve a high performance these recommendations stemmed from the factors which were identi ed using algorithm 2 the dashboard is delivered to the students at the beginning of the 6 688 p 0 0001 in group 1 students performance while group 2 students frontiers in arti cial intelligence www frontiersin org difference was not signi cant t 2 026 p 0 055 as shown in both statistical analyses the dashboard positively impacted students learning and helped them reach the desired academic performance 5 discussion the purpose of this study was to propose an explainable mlbased approach in la to predict student performance at an assessment level and to identify which factors affect student performance we also aimed to implement and evaluate the proposed approach as a dfiar dashboard to examine its utility and limitations for students we discuss our results and the implications of these ndings in the following sections 5 1 findings and implications the rst aim was to explore how student performance could be accurately predicted at the assignment or quiz level using established ml algorithms we found that random forestbased predictive models provided satisfying results when utilising the education data of students taking online programming courses since prediction is entirely dependent on the data supplied we attempted to identify the association between data variables and academic achievement we found that active participation in an lms quiz score and assignment grade attributes were essential to determining student academic performance because they were positively correlated with student performance throughout the course however the importance of the initial assessment attributes decreased during the middle of the course due to the additional attributes such as practical videos and assignments one of the practical implications of these ndings is that prediction at 16 november 2021 volume 4 article 723447 afzaal et al explainable ai for intelligent feedback the assessment level increases students interest in learning and motivates them to adapt the course material and learning paths to meet their needs better such predictions could also support teachers in engaging in timely interventions to help students who are predicted to achieve low results these prediction ndings led us to the rst research question can we employ explainable ml approaches to identify factors that affect students academic performance at the assignment or quiz level in order to provide automatic and data driven feedback as illustrated in the results section we found that explainable ml was not only able to identify the potentially in uencing factors from courses currently running but it was also able to identify the necessary change in the feature value to reach high performance moreover we found ve factors such as active participation in the lms forum discussion programming experience quiz score and assignment grade that dominated students academic performance the required value change in in uencing factors provided an additional edge to the proposed approach against existing approaches to factor identi cation akhtar et al 2017 lu et al 2018 ahuja et al 2019 bibi et al 2019 kamal and ahuja 2019 which were also able to identify the factors but were not able to calculate the required value change to reach a high performance on an individual level since changing the value of one factor could affect the whole prediction the appropriate estimation of the value change for each prediction helped to calculate the real impact of each factor the proposed approach utilised the accurate performance prediction and identi ed factors along with their impact and required change as shown in figure 3 to develop a dashboard for the data driven feedback and action recommendations the prediction and factor identi cation ndings led us to the second research question what is the perceived utility and limitations of the dashboard for data driven feedback and action recommendations for students as presented in the dashboard evaluation results section we found three main bene ts first the dashboard helped students to self regulate especially when the course structure is complex and students have to read and watch extensive course material in this case the dashboard assisted students regulation of learning by providing action recommendations that highlighted the course resources the students should focus on next in order to increase the probability of improved course performance moreover the outline of recommendations along with the progress bar provided allowed students to monitor their progress and plan adjustments to improve their learning process the second bene t concerned the level of motivation to learn by providing data driven feedback in terms of estimated assessment scores the provision of assessment scores after following a recommendation was found to be an interesting aspect of the dashboard that motivated students and increased their interest in following more recommendations another motivational aspect which was revealed from the results regarding the dashboard interface and was found to be easy to use and interpretable by students was the dashboard s friendly interface this also frontiers in arti cial intelligence www frontiersin org motivated students to engage in their studies leading to enhanced learning outcomes yet another identi ed bene t was related to the impact generated when following action recommendations although the sample of students was relatively small in this study a signi cant correlation was found between the number of recommendations followed and students nal course performance in terms of limitations the dashboard is unable to provide evidence about whether the recommendations followed improved student knowledge about course concepts or not for example after following a recommendation the dashboard does not provide any mechanism such as a questionnaire to students so that they can verify that knowledge has been constructed assimilated based on the recommendation followed moreover the dashboard interface is limited to providing a predictive performance of the students as it does not display the highest scores in the course and does not allow students to compare their current learning with that of their peers these ndings are interesting from four perspectives from the student s perspective a potential practical implication of the ndings of this work is that the students improve their learning outcomes by self monitoring of their progress it leads them to complete their courses and achieve the desired educational goals from the perspective of teachers these ndings are helpful to save teacher time by providing students with a self regulatory environment that aware students of their learning status and guide them regarding suitable learning material individually this assistance to teachers reduces their workload and helps to improve their other pedagogical practices such as enhancing course structure content and course related activities from the institutions perspective these ndings are helpful to improve students retention rate by providing timely guidance in terms of their predictive assessment scores it causes that student s rate of dropping out is declined and they ultimately can achieve their course degree at the time however lack of student s self regulation causes many pedagogical and societal issues such as teachers have to make much effort to deliver appropriate instructions to each student regarding the study content in a course similarly by increasing the dropout rate on the one hand most students are failed that causes them to be psychologically demoralized on the other hand state money invested in different education programs is wasted from a generalizability perspective we claim that the proposed approach is quite applicable to diverse educational courses to apply the approach to a new course all possible modalities of data for a new course e g quizzes assignments practical exercises watched videos reading material project tasks and nal exams are taken as input then a feature analysis including feature extraction and selection is performed again except on common features such as lms usage and motivation level since features are speci c to courses the ml model is rebuilt and could then predict student academic performance accurately afterwards the lime framework can be employed on the built ml model and extracted features to identify the in uencing factors lastly identi ed factors can 17 november 2021 volume 4 article 723447 afzaal et al explainable ai for intelligent feedback 6 conclusion be used to provide intelligent feedback and action recommendations on a dashboard in this paper we have proposed an explainable ml based approach to provide automatic and intelligent effective feedback and action recommendations for students in this approach an explainable ml based algorithm has been developed that utilises students lms data and builds predictive models to compute data driven feedback and recommendations for action at the assignment or quiz level which can help students to self regulate their learning and improve their academic performance to examine the effectiveness of the proposed approach a dashboard was designed developed and implemented in a real course setting evaluation of the implemented dashboard was conducted by identifying the utility and bene ts of the dashboard evaluation results showed that the dashboard helped students in selfregulation boosting their motivation and improving their academic performance in the future we will perform experiments on larger data sets to ensure that the proposed approach is sustainable and we will not need to resample the data to avoid data imbalance problem moreover we will collaborate with course teachers to deploy and evaluate our dashboards in massive courses to determine their ef cacy 5 2 limitations and future recommendations in terms of limitations this paper performs experiments on a programming course that limits its generalizability but we see that generalizability is not negatively affected due to two reasons first model building in the proposed approach was on a very general across subject didactical structure because the participants were from different disciplines such as mathematics social sciences and electrical engineering second the developed recommender dashboard can be used in diverse online courses as it was based on a very speci c way of designing an online course that consisted of all imaginable online course components such as videos audios assignments and quizzes etc and allows the students to follow them in a chronological temporal order the second main limitation is about sample size for experimentation the experimental set for evaluation of the recommender system consisted of only 34 participants however in the future we plan to perform an evaluation at a large scale with big sample size in our future work we will emphasize how to improve the utility of the dashboard by adding more functionality and easier to use design components in its interface furthermore the confronted challenges and limitations such as generalizability will also be stressed to work on in the future prospect one other future direction is to make a dashboard for teachers that could be useful in pedagogical practices in this dashboard recommendations will be provided to teachers while providing helpful instructions in their study moreover the used lime framework provides a local explanation or local in uences of features that give importance to features in a particular observation instead of providing a global in uence in which the overall importance of features for the predictive model is provided since this drawback of the lime framework affects the quality of data driven feedback and action recommendations provided on the dashboard one of our future directions will be the provision of the global in uence of features to improve recommendations for actions furthermore data anonymization is among our future directions so that the data processing steps can enter the scrutiny of a public dataset data availability statement the datasets presented in this article are not readily available because dataset was collected to improve university students performance and for course improvements therefore it will not available to the public requests to access the datasets should be directed to chapter 3 methodology 3 1 research design this chapter sets out what was planned for the study and why chapter 4 reports what was actually built and how chapter 5 reports what happened when the system was tested and chapter 6 discusses what those results mean where the final evaluation departed from the original plan this chapter describes the final method and records the planned but unimplemented elements in section 3 4 1 this study adopts the commonkads knowledge engineering ke methodology as its primary knowledge engineering and design framework schreiber et al 2000 studer et al 1998 commonkads was selected because the main design problem in this study is a knowledge engineering problem how to represent and communicate the knowledge produced by the prediction system in particular the study examines how shap and lime explanations can be presented to instructors advisors and administrators according to their different information needs commonkads was developed for analysing and designing knowledge intensive systems schreiber et al 2000 this makes it suitable for the present study which uses lms data to generate predictions and xai explanations for different stakeholder roles schreiber et al 2000 structure commonkads as six models covering organisational context tasks agents knowledge communication and system design each model addresses a specific design requirement in this study for the present study the organisation model captures the institutional context of lms use and identifies how at risk prediction information currently flows between instructors advisors and administrators as well as identifying where that flow breaks down the task model decomposes the overall at risk prediction and explanation task into sub tasks risk assessment explanation generation role assignment and explanation delivery the agent model characterises each stakeholder role s knowledge capabilities and explanation needs informing differentiated interface designs the knowledge model formalises the domain knowledge underlying at risk prediction including the behavioural and demographic features identified by the predictive model and their relative contributions as quantified by shap the communication model specifies the interaction patterns between each agent role and the system the design model maps these knowledge engineering components onto the technical architecture on the pragmatics of explanation which argues that effective explanations are contrastive selective and audience sensitive the design model then translates these upstream models into the layered technical architecture developed in section 3 2 this approach ensures that commonkads guides system design rather than serving only as a descriptive framework organisation model because no institutional partner was involved the organisation model was constructed from published accounts rather than from an organisational study in the as is situation described in this literature at risk predictions reach institutional staff as risk scores presented in isolation without an account of the reasoning behind them susnjak et al 2022 dashboards are typically designed for a single archetypal user kaliisa et al 2023 and a shortage of practitioner facing decision support is one of the barriers to institutional adoption tsai ga evi 2017 the flow of at risk information therefore breaks down at two points when a prediction reaches a practitioner without an explanation they can check against what they know and when a single view requires each role to aggregate or disaggregate the information before it becomes usable in the to be situation specified for this study instructors advisors and administrators receive the same underlying prediction and explanation at the granularity relevant to each role s decision while the practitioner retains the intervention decision the secondary theoretical lens is the technology acceptance model tam developed by davis 1989 which frames user adoption of information systems around perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use tam davis 1989 informs the design goals for each role specific interface its two core constructs perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use providing a simple but well validated basis for reasoning about what a usable adoptable dashboard interface should offer each stakeholder role complementing the user need framing established in the commonkads agent and communication models because this study is scoped to secondary oulad data rather than primary practitioner data collection section 3 8 tam is used solely as a design lens not as an empirical framework a tam based practitioner evaluation is identified in chapter 7 as future work the research proceeds through four iterative phases knowledge acquisition and organisation analysis knowledge and system modelling artefact design and development and technical evaluation the choice of tam as a secondary lens is deliberate not incidental venkatesh and bala 2008 extended the original tam into tam3 by consolidating a broad body of empirical evidence on the antecedents of perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use and their meta analytic findings continue to support the predictive value of these constructs for professional software adoption maranguni and grani 2015 reviewed 85 tam studies and concluded that the model remains the most consistently supported framework for evaluating information system acceptance across educational and workplace contexts tam is therefore used alongside the commonkads agent and communication models tam contributes the constructs of perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use while the agent and communication models describe the information needs of each stakeholder role kim et al 2024 identify the same constructs as central to how ai explanations are received which makes them relevant to a future practitioner evaluation the study also draws on the design science paradigm described by hevner et al 2004 which peffers et al 2007 later developed into the design science research methodology both argue that research centred on a purposeful artefact is justified by the rigour of its construction and by its usefulness when evaluated against a well defined problem this fits the present study which contributes a working dashboard and design guidelines derived from its evaluation this study adopts the iterative process proposed by peffers et al 2007 alongside commonkads it comprises problem identification objective definition design and development demonstration evaluation and communication commonkads guides the knowledge modelling activities within each phase while dsrm provides the overall structure for conducting the research the frameworks therefore serve different purposes in the study the design science research methodology dsrm is the overarching research paradigm and process commonkads is the knowledge engineering and design framework applied within that process tam is a theoretical lens for anticipated technology acceptance and the kaliisa et al 2023 checklist provides dashboard design guidance none of these frameworks other than dsrm serves as the overarching methodology and tam is not evaluated empirically the four iterative phases identified above are conducted with explicit feedback loops between them rather than as a strict linear progression in this study knowledge acquisition drew on published literature rather than user based elicitation so findings from the literature review fed into the modelling phase where an agent characterisation was refined and outputs from the technical evaluation could inform late adjustments to the design phase this iterative structure is consistent with the recommendations of verbert et al 2013 who caution that dashboard design in learning analytics must accommodate revisions arising from user studies rather than freezing design decisions at an early stage because no user studies were conducted here such revisions are left to the future practitioner evaluation outlined in chapter 7 3 2 system architecture the overall system architecture adopted in this study is illustrated in figure 3 2 the process begins with problem identification and literature review followed by commonkads knowledge engineering dataset selection and preparation using oulad predictive modelling with ensemble machine learning explainability integration using shap and lime system implementation using react and flask role based dashboard design technical evaluation of predictive performance and explanation behaviour against oulad and concludes with the development of design guidelines figure 3 2 research process flowchart from problem identification through evaluation and derivation of design guidelines this system s architecture is driven by the need to address two established limitations in the literature first existing student at risk prediction systems emphasise predictive accuracy while offering limited interpretability thereby constraining their usefulness in practice ali et al 2023 second most learning analytics dashboards adopt uniform interface designs despite clear evidence that different stakeholder roles require different forms of analytical insight kaliisa et al 2023 kostopoulos et al 2024 the architecture therefore separates data processing prediction explanation and user interaction ensuring each component directly addresses these limitations the overall system is organised into five separate architectural layers namely the data layer the prediction engine the explainability module the role assignment and personalisation layer and the presentation layer communication between layers is mediated by well defined interfaces implemented as restful endpoints which allow each layer to be revised replaced or scaled without cascading changes throughout the system this architectural design is consistent with the guidance of bass et al 2021 and aligns with the recommendations of adadi and berrada 2018 who argue that explainable ai systems benefit from architectures in which the explanation component is treated as a core part of the system rather than being added after model development figure 3 3 layered system architecture separating data prediction explanation personalization and presentation concerns a layered architectural approach is adopted because modular separation improves system clarity scalability and integration of explainability mechanisms in ai systems barredo arrieta et al 2020 mohseni et al 2021 this is particularly necessary in this study as post hoc explanation techniques such as shap and lime operate independently of the predictive model and require flexible integration within the system pipeline ali et al 2023 salih et al 2025 the choice of a layered rather than pipeline only architecture is also motivated by the need to accommodate concurrent use instructors advisors and administrators may access the dashboard simultaneously and request explanations at different granularities and computationally expensive explanation queries could otherwise delay simpler cohort level requests separating the explanation service from the presentation logic and pre computing the most expensive shap outputs is intended to avoid this bottleneck the specific implementation is described in chapter 4 the data layer is defined as a separate component to ensure consistency in feature extraction and preprocessing this is justified by evidence that lms behavioural logs demographic variables and assessment data are the most reliable predictors of student risk guevara reyes et al 2025 jin et al 2024 kuzilek et al 2017 wang 2025 isolating this layer supports reproducibility and reduces variability in feature engineering a source of inconsistency in prior studies jin et al 2024 the data layer is also responsible for temporally aligning interaction records with assessment deadlines a step essential for constructing time window features following the temporal feature construction strategies documented by hlosta et al 2017 interaction counts are aggregated over rolling windows anchored to submission dates rather than over calendar weeks because deadline anchored windows have been shown to yield stronger early warning signals than calendar anchored windows on oulad this treatment also lets the same feature pipeline be reused for both training and inference without leaking future information into historical windows a concern emphasised by krstajic et al 2014 in their analysis of cross validation pitfalls in predictive modelling the prediction engine is implemented as an independent layer to support ensemble learning methods ensemble models have consistently demonstrated superior predictive performance in at risk classification tasks rebelo marcolino et al 2025 wang 2025 however their increased complexity reduces interpretability necessitating a dedicated explanation component guevara reyes et al 2025 the explainability module addresses this requirement by converting model outputs into interpretable representations the combined use of shap and lime is based on prior studies reporting complementary strengths with shap commonly used for global attribution and lime for local explanations of individual predictions gunasekara saarela 2025 nnadi et al 2024 salih et al 2025 this ensures that the module adequately addresses both cohort level and instance level interpretation needs the explainability module includes two internal sub services the first a global explanation service computes and caches treeshap values lundberg et al 2020 across the training population these values underpin the cohort level visualisations used by administrators and at a coarser grain by advisors the second a local explanation service generates on demand lime approximations for individual predictions ribeiro et al 2016 and produces a corresponding local shap explanation using the tree path dependent estimator so the two techniques can be compared side by side within the interface storing global shap outputs while computing lime on demand reflects the difference in computing time between the two methods reported by salih et al 2025 where shap has higher computing time than lime global shap outputs can be cached and reused whereas lime which relies on perturbation and repeated model evaluations must be regenerated for each new instance figure 3 4 dual service explainability pipeline global treeshap is pre computed and cached while lime and local shap are generated on demand the role based interface layer is introduced to resolve the limitation of role agnostic dashboard design prior studies show that explanation effectiveness depends on alignment with user roles and decision contexts guti rrez et al 2020 haque et al 2023 kostopoulos et al 2024 accordingly the system maps shared explanation outputs to role specific visualisations for instructors advisors and administrators this allows a single predictive model to support multiple stakeholders without redundancy and is intended to support each role s decision making its effect on usability was not measured in this study figure 3 5 mapping of shared prediction and explanation outputs to instructor advisor and administrator dashboard views the mapping between shared explanation outputs and role specific visualisations is implemented as a configurable presentation policy rather than as hard coded logic this design decision follows the recommendation of sokol and flach 2020 that explanation systems adopt a modular fact sheet based approach in which the choice of explanation type granularity and format is decoupled from the underlying model each stakeholder role in the present system is associated with a policy specifying the explanation granularity cohort group or individual the visualisation modality aggregated bar chart per student breakdown or narrative summary and the level of technical detail exposed this makes it possible to introduce additional roles in future work without altering the prediction or explanation services the presentation layer is treated as a distinct concern rather than as a thin rendering shell over the role assignment policy its responsibilities include composing visual components managing interaction state and translating explanation artefacts into forms that respect the cognitive constraints of the intended audience hern ndez leo et al 2019 emphasise that the visualisation layer of a learning analytics system is where design decisions become directly observable to end users and that weaknesses at this layer often mask the value of otherwise sound analytical pipelines accordingly the presentation layer in this study is developed as a component library organised around three primitives the risk indicator the feature attribution panel and the cohort comparison view each parameterised by the presentation policy handed down from the role assignment layer a second reason for isolating the presentation layer is the need to accommodate accessibility and progressive disclosure miteva and stefanova 2022 in their model of a learning analytics visualisation system note that dashboards for heterogeneous audiences benefit from layered disclosure in which summary indicators appear first and technical detail is revealed on demand the presentation layer implements this pattern by rendering compact risk summaries as the default view for every role and by exposing shap and lime visualisations only when the user requests a deeper explanation this behaviour is delegated entirely to the interface tier so the explainability module remains agnostic to downstream visualisation choices the interaction among these layers follows a structured data flow in which lms data is processed transformed into predictions interpreted through post hoc explanations and delivered through role specific visualisation logic this design ensures consistency flexibility and alignment with stakeholder needs the architecture is therefore justified as a knowledge engineering solution that integrates modular design explainability and role awareness to address the limitations of existing systems implementation details of each layer including feature dictionaries model manifests and caching are reported in chapter 4 rather than here a supporting architectural diagram is produced as part of the commonkads design model to make the described data flow explicit in the diagram the data layer feeds pre processed feature vectors into the prediction engine which returns risk probabilities to both the explainability module and the role assignment layer the explainability module returns cached global shap artefacts and freshly generated local explanations to the presentation layer which composes them into role appropriate views the presentation layer enforces authentication and authorisation so a practitioner is exposed only to the interface and explanation granularity associated with their role this end to end trace is intended to satisfy the reproducibility criterion proposed by gundersen and kjensmo 2018 who argue that machine learning research artefacts should permit an independent reviewer to reconstruct the pipeline from raw data to end user output 3 3 dataset the open university learning analytics dataset oulad is adopted as the primary dataset for model development kuzilek et al 2017 this selection is justified by its extensive use in the literature which enables direct comparison with prior studies and strengthens the validity of the results gunasekara saarela 2025 jin et al 2024 wang 2025 since its release oulad has become one of the most widely used benchmarks for at risk prediction research and has therefore accumulated an unusually rich body of comparative evidence hlosta et al 2017 provide one of the earliest baseline analyses of the dataset and document the class distributions the temporal structure of the interaction logs and the operational meaning of the pass fail and withdrawn labels subsequent contributions from waheed et al 2020 and from adnan et al 2021 have extended this baseline with deep learning treatments and time series formulations respectively and their published performance figures provide credible reference points against which the models developed in this study can be benchmarked adopting oulad therefore also situates the present study within a live comparative research programme oulad contains anonymised demographic data and aggregated virtual learning environment interaction records for 32 593 student module presentation observations across 22 module presentations kuzilek et al 2017 these data types correspond directly to the feature categories most frequently identified as predictive of student at risk status jin et al 2024 kuzilek et al 2017 the dataset is therefore appropriate for the binary classification task adopted in this study the dataset is composed of seven relational tables covering student registrations demographic attributes module presentations assessments assessment results vle resources and vle interaction logs and these tables are joined on student and module identifiers to produce the analytical dataset used for modelling waheed et al 2020 report that the interaction table alone contains over ten million records providing the volume necessary for stable estimation of high capacity ensemble models the demographic attributes include age band gender region highest prior education index of multiple deprivation band disability status and number of previous attempts all of which have been shown in prior work to carry non trivial predictive signal adnan et al 2021 kuzilek et al 2017 because several of these attributes are also protected characteristics under educational equity frameworks their inclusion is treated as a design decision with fairness implications discussed further in section 3 9 oulad is further justified by its scale completeness and ethical suitability its anonymised structure eliminates concerns relating to personally identifiable information while its size supports the development of robust and generalisable models the dataset is therefore selected for its relevance comparability and methodological consistency with existing research data preparation proceeded through five stages the first stage performs schema validation and referential integrity checks across the seven source tables the second stage constructs the analytical target variable by collapsing the four class final result field into a binary at risk indicator mapping withdrawn and fail to the positive class and pass and distinction to the negative class following the convention adopted by jin et al 2024 in their systematic review of oulad based studies the third stage generates cumulative and rolling window interaction features anchored on assessment deadlines following the temporal aggregation strategy described by hlosta et al 2017 the fourth stage encodes the categorical attributes including module gender region highest education index of multiple deprivation band age band and disability using one hot representations chapter 5 section 5 2 the fifth stage records the course presentation code presentation for each observation so cross validation folds can be grouped by presentation mitigating the risk of optimistic estimates from ignoring the data s panel structure a concern raised by rebelo marcolino et al 2025 in their optimisation study of moodle log data missing values are handled in two ways assessment and interaction counts are set to zero where a student has no recorded submissions or activity because no record means no activity any remaining missing values such as a missing index of multiple deprivation band are filled inside the model pipeline with the median for numeric features and the most frequent category for categorical ones fitted on the training folds only so that no information passes from the validation data van buuren 2018 notes that indicator encoding can be preferable to simple imputation when missingness may itself be informative a condition that is plausible for administrative educational data so adding missingness indicators is a possible refinement 3 4 predictive modelling the predictive modelling task is formulated as a binary classification problem where students are classified as at risk if they withdraw or fail their module this formulation is consistent with established approaches in the literature and supports practical intervention scenarios jin et al 2024 the binary formulation is preferred over multi class or regression alternatives for two principled reasons first the classifier supports an immediate screening decision whether to flag a student for further consideration albreiki et al 2021 report that most oulad based studies reviewed in their systematic analysis adopt a comparable binary framing the intervention that may follow a flag is not binary since an instructor or advisor might contact the student monitor refer provide resources adjust teaching escalate or do nothing and that decision remains with the practitioner second a binary target avoids the label ambiguity that arises when pass and distinction are treated as distinct classes since prior work has shown that the boundary between these two categories is more sensitive to marking conventions across module presentations than to underlying behavioural differences kuzilek et al 2017 prior studies identify submission timeliness vle interaction frequency assessment performance trends and demographic indicators as key predictors of student outcomes guevara reyes et al 2025 wang 2025 selecting these features aligns with existing empirical findings and supports interpretability the engineered feature set is organised into three thematic families to preserve interpretability at the presentation layer the engagement family captures aggregate and time windowed counts of clicks by vle activity type following the taxonomy of resource categories documented in the oulad schema kuzilek et al 2017 the assessment family captures scores achieved on tutor marked and computer marked assessments together with submission latency computed as the interval between assessment release and submission following the timeliness features shown by hussain et al 2018 to be strongly associated with subsequent module outcomes the demographic family captures the encoded demographic attributes described in section 3 3 each engineered feature is documented with a human readable label and a short explanatory phrase in a feature dictionary so that the presentation layer can render meaningful labels rather than variable names when surfacing shap and lime attributions this study compares three ensemble models random forest xgboost and gradient boosting classifier ensemble methods are justified by their demonstrated superiority in predictive performance across multiple studies rebelo marcolino et al 2025 wang 2025 f1 score is used for comparative reporting because it provides a balanced measure of performance in the presence of class imbalance jin et al 2024 the model deployed in the prototype however is selected with recall as the primary criterion and f1 score as a secondary metric because recall is prioritised to reduce false negatives in the intended screening context a student who is at risk but not flagged receives no support from the dashboard whereas a student who is flagged unnecessarily is reviewed by a practitioner and can be set aside the three candidate models are chosen because they represent distinct points along the bias variance and interpretability spectra recognised in the machine learning literature random forest as formulated by breiman 2001 reduces variance by averaging deep decorrelated trees and remains a widely regarded strong general purpose baseline for tabular classification xgboost introduced by t chen and guestrin 2016 applies regularised gradient boosting on decision trees and has become the reference implementation for boosting on structured data particularly with heterogeneous feature types the gradient boosting classifier as implemented in scikit learn following friedman 2001 provides a more conservative boosting baseline against which the xgboost configuration can be compared this three way comparison follows the pattern established by rebelo marcolino et al 2025 and by guevara reyes et al 2025 both of whom argue that credible ensemble evaluations require at least one bagging model and at least two boosting models to isolate the effects of the ensembling strategy from those of the boosting refinements the final evaluation used four fold groupkfold cross validation grouped by course presentation code presentation so observations from the same presentation never appear in both the training and validation partitions of a fold avoiding the leakage pattern criticised by krstajic et al 2014 because oulad contains four course presentations this produces four folds and the folds are not stratified since stratification is not compatible with grouping on a variable that takes only four values the xgboost model deployed in the prototype was evaluated using a fixed configuration 300 estimators maximum depth 5 learning rate 0 05 subsample 0 8 and column subsample 0 8 without additional hyperparameter optimisation or resampling and random forest and gradient boosting were evaluated under the identical preprocessing pipeline and protocol accuracy precision recall and f1 score computed over out of fold predictions at a decision threshold of 0 5 are the primary metrics and the training code also records roc auc 3 4 1 planned but not implemented methodological extensions the original study design specified several refinements to the modelling and evaluation pipeline that were not implemented in the final evaluation they are recorded here so that this chapter describes the final method accurately while remaining transparent about the original plan chapter 2 section 2 2 reviews the literature motivating each refinement class imbalance handling smote including borderline and adaptive variants applied within the training folds and class weighted loss functions were specified as ways of addressing class imbalance neither was applied because the final evaluation used the observed class distribution which is only mildly imbalanced chapter 5 section 5 2 hyperparameter optimisation bayesian optimisation with the tree structured parzen estimator was specified for hyperparameter search the prototype model instead used the fixed configuration described above probability calibration a comparison of isotonic regression and platt scaling assessed through reliability diagrams and expected calibration error was specified because the dashboard displays risk probabilities calibration was not assessed in the final evaluation trajectory features a trajectory feature family capturing period over period change in engagement and performance was specified the implemented feature set does not include it secondary metrics area under the precision recall curve balanced accuracy and the matthews correlation coefficient were specified as secondary metrics and were not computed in the final evaluation cross validation protocol the original design described a stratified five fold protocol it was superseded by the four fold groupkfold protocol described above which is the method used in the final evaluation explanation stability and fidelity and subgroup fairness the stability and fidelity checks for explanations section 3 5 and the subgroup performance and fairness assessment section 3 9 were proposed but were not completed within the final evaluation 3 5 explainability integration integrating explainable ai techniques is necessary to address the limited interpretability of predictive models in educational contexts prior research indicates that risk predictions without explanation provide limited support for decision making ahmed et al 2025 ali et al 2023 the explanation subsystem design is grounded in the distinction doshi velez and kim 2017 draw between transparency oriented and post hoc interpretability transparency oriented approaches require the model itself to be intrinsically understandable which typically constrains model choice to linear models or shallow trees at a substantial cost in accuracy post hoc approaches in contrast decouple the interpretability question from the modelling question and allow high capacity models to be deployed alongside a dedicated explanation layer adadi and berrada 2018 argue that in domains such as education where the accuracy of the underlying model has direct consequences for the students subject to intervention the post hoc route is generally preferable provided the resulting explanations undergo explicit fidelity and stability testing this position underpins the decision in the present study to retain ensemble models and to invest architectural effort in the explanation layer shap is used for global model interpretation while lime is used for local explanations this combination is justified by studies reporting that shap provides consistent feature attribution while lime offers flexible and interpretable explanations for individual instances gunasekara saarela 2025 nnadi et al 2024 salih et al 2025 the use of both techniques ensures that explanations are available at different levels of analysis shap is grounded in the game theoretic framework of shapley values and is implemented in this study using the treeshap algorithm proposed by lundberg et al 2020 which computes exact shapley values for tree ensembles in polynomial time and thereby renders the method tractable for the oulad scale feature space lime introduced by ribeiro et al 2016 fits a sparse linear surrogate to the behaviour of the model in the local neighbourhood of a given prediction and returns the surrogate coefficients as feature level explanations the two methods are complementary rather than redundant shap is formulated to satisfy properties such as local accuracy and consistency lundberg lee 2017 although these properties depend on the exact shap formulation and its assumptions including the assumption of feature independence discussed by salih et al 2025 whereas lime provides a more intuitive linear approximation that many practitioners find easier to reason about in isolation salih et al 2025 argue explicitly for the joint use of both techniques as a form of methodological triangulation and this argument is adopted here the explanation subsystem was also designed to incorporate safeguards against the known failure modes of post hoc methods slack et al 2020 show that shap and lime can be manipulated by adversarial classifiers to conceal discriminatory behaviour and although the present study does not confront an adversarial setting the same underlying sensitivity to perturbation choices motivates reporting stability metrics the methodology proposed quantifying stability using the jaccard similarity of the top k feature sets returned by repeated lime runs on the same instance with different random seeds following the protocol of visani et al 2022 and quantifying fidelity using the local squared error between the surrogate and the black box model within a locality kernel of controlled bandwidth with instances falling below preregistered thresholds flagged in the interface these stability and fidelity checks were proposed safeguards rather than completed evaluation procedures they were not completed in the final evaluation and the explanation evaluation reported in chapter 5 is limited to cross method agreement between shap and lime shap values are pre computed during model training and stored to support efficient retrieval lime explanations are generated on demand for individual predictions enabling real time interaction within the dashboard explanation quality was evaluated through cross method agreement between shap and lime the fidelity and stability metrics described above were specified but not completed the presentation of explanations is shaped by the pragmatics of explanation set out by miller 2019 whose synthesis of social science research on how humans give and receive explanations identifies three properties that any effective explanation must satisfy explanations should be contrastive clarifying why a particular outcome was predicted rather than a plausible alternative explanations should be selective surfacing the small number of factors that most strongly account for the outcome rather than the full attribution vector explanations should be social in that they should be phrased in terms accessible to the intended recipient the presentation layer draws on these selective and social properties by rendering per instance explanations as signed feature attributions limited to a small set of leading features with human readable feature labels at an aggregation level suited to the associated stakeholder role the prototype implements feature attributions rather than contrastive or counterfactual explanations and it does not include natural language comparative statements therefore the contrastive property remains a design aspiration rather than a feature of the current system this aligns the explanation experience with the empirical evidence of poursabzi sangdeh et al 2021 who show that human comprehension of model outputs degrades sharply when unfiltered attribution vectors are displayed in full 3 6 dashboard design the dashboard design process was structured by the four stage checklist of kaliisa et al 2023 which guides developers from initial purpose specification and stakeholder engagement through iterative prototyping and rigorous evaluation planning a sequence directly applicable to the three role design problem of this study this checklist was selected because it was developed explicitly for learning analytics contexts and has been applied in subsequent la dashboard research cabral et al 2025 three role specific interface variants were designed and implemented as a web application using react js with a python flask backend interface decisions were guided by the heuristic criteria set out below and checked against the commonkads agent model consistent with the secondary data scope of this study section 3 8 no documented iterative heuristic review with recorded iterations reviewers or severity ratings was conducted the design process was structured by the commonkads design model so that each interface variant maps directly to the knowledge delivery requirements identified for its corresponding agent role each interface was designed around a separate information brief derived from the commonkads agent model the instructor interface focuses on class level engagement during the current teaching period and provides explanations of individual students risk drivers using assessment and weekly activity data following the information needs identified by molenaar and knoop van campen 2019 in their study of teacher facing dashboards the advisor interface prioritises longitudinal views across multiple modules for a caseload of students foregrounding demographic context in a form suitable for one to one consultations in line with the design pattern used by guti rrez et al 2020 in the lada advising system the administrator interface prioritises cohort level aggregations module over module comparisons and equity relevant breakdowns following the institutional decision support patterns documented by tsai and ga evi 2017 these role specific briefs prevent the dashboard from using the same view for all users table 3 2 summarises the resulting role based design table 3 2 role based dashboard design decisions information needs components and explanation granularity role decision information needed dashboard component explanation granularity instructor whether to act within a course that is currently running class level engagement over the current teaching period and per student risk drivers at the granularity of assessments and weekly activity per student reasoning trail with shap and lime shown side by side individual advisor how to conduct a conversation with a particular student and prioritise a caseload views across multiple modules for a caseload of students with demographic context suitable for one to one consultations cohort averaged reasoning trail for students at or above the watch threshold caseload administrator where to direct institutional attention and resource cohort level aggregations and module over module comparisons institution wide model performance summary and full population reasoning trail cohort the interface follows nielsen s 1994 human computer interaction heuristics particularly visibility of system status match between the system and the real world recognition rather than recall and consistency and standards colour usage is designed to remain informative for practitioners with common forms of colour vision deficiency by using colour blind safe palettes and encoding critical categorical distinctions redundantly through shape and label following the accessible visualisation guidance synthesised by munzner 2014 typography spacing and interactive controls were designed with reference to the wcag 2 1 conformance criteria of the world wide web consortium which is consistent with the accessibility first orientation increasingly expected of higher education software the study did not conduct a formal iterative heuristic review with documented iterations reviewers or severity ratings instead the nielsen 1994 criteria were applied as design guidance during implementation a formal heuristic evaluation together with a formative think aloud study with representative practitioners of the kind recommended by verbert et al 2020 is identified in chapter 7 as future work once the dashboard is evaluated with an institutional partner a system architecture diagram was produced during the design phase to illustrate the data flow from raw lms input through the prediction engine explainability module and role based interface layer this diagram serves as the principal artefact of the commonkads design model figure 3 3 and figure 4 1 the design plan also specified three supporting artefacts a use case diagram enumerating the primary interactions available to each role produced in the unified modelling language following the notation of booch et al 2005 an entity relationship diagram capturing the persistent data model that underlies the data layer and a sequence diagram illustrating the runtime interaction between the presentation layer the prediction engine and the explainability module for a representative on demand explanation request these supporting diagrams are not included in the thesis figures 3 3 and 4 1 therefore provide the main architectural documentation presented in the study 3 7 implementation plan the system was implemented using python for all data processing model training and explainability computation with scikit learn xgboost shap and lime as the primary libraries these libraries were selected based on their suitability for the required tasks scikit learn is adopted for its consistent estimator interface and its well tested implementations of cross validation preprocessing and model evaluation utilities as documented by pedregosa et al 2011 xgboost was selected because of its regularised objective sparsity aware split finding and out of core training capabilities t chen guestrin 2016 shap is adopted through its official reference implementation to guarantee alignment with the theoretical guarantees of treeshap established by lundberg et al 2020 lime is adopted through the reference implementation of ribeiro et al 2016 the library versions used in the evaluation are reported in chapter 5 section 5 7 and in appendix a in line with the reproducibility recommendations of gundersen and kjensmo 2018 the web application was built using react js for the frontend and python flask for the api layer a combination selected because it enables rapid prototyping of interactive visualisation components alongside a well tested machine learning pipeline the code was organised into separate modules for the prediction explainability and visualisation components chapter 4 section 4 3 the three role specific interfaces were implemented as web pages within a single application with role based authentication determining which view a practitioner accesses upon login the frontend is organised as a component based application using the composition principles articulated in the react documentation of meta open source 2024 and the maintainability guidance of martin 2017 visualisation components are implemented using the d3 based ecosystem drawing on the grammar of interactive graphics described by satyanarayan et al 2017 which supports the declarative construction of coordinated views necessary for exploratory dashboards the flask backend exposes rest endpoints for prediction global explanation retrieval and local explanation generation and implements authentication using json web tokens following the specification of jones et al 2015 role based access control is enforced at the api layer and the interface layer consistent with the defence in depth principle articulated by saltzer and schroeder 1975 so the interface layer is not the sole enforcement point for role separation the planned testing strategy included several levels of testing unit tests for the preprocessing pipeline model wrappers and explanation utilities integration tests for the api contracts between the frontend and the backend and regression tests for the explanation subsystem to detect unexpected shifts in shap and lime outputs following library upgrades which matters because slack et al 2020 demonstrate that explanation methods are sensitive to implementation details that may change silently across versions continuous integration was also planned following the software delivery practices described by humble and farley 2010 this testing and continuous integration pipeline is not demonstrated in this thesis and is therefore described as planned practice rather than completed infrastructure the prototype source code is held in a version controlled git repository https github com daniel larry role aware xai dashboard including the data preparation model training and explanation code the flask api the react dashboard the moodle plugin the docker compose configuration the feature dictionary and the model manifest the trained model and the shap cache are not stored in the repository they are rebuilt from the oulad files when the prototype is first started chapter 4 section 4 11 the repository also contains an environment configuration file with test only credentials for the local docker services included so that other reviewers can run the prototype without further setup these credentials are not used in any institutional system a formal archive of the code trained model artefacts and derived data with a persistent identifier in accordance with the fair data principles articulated by wilkinson et al 2016 has not been made 3 8 evaluation plan consistent with the scope of this study section 1 6 evaluation is a technical evaluation of the predictive and explanatory components against the oulad dataset rather than a primary study involving instructor advisor or administrator participants the evaluation plan below specifies what is measured how and against what standard of comparison predictive performance is evaluated using groupkfold cross validation grouped by course presentation code presentation this ensures that the model does not train on the same presentation used for evaluation because oulad contains four course presentations this produces four folds metrics are computed over out of fold predictions across the full population accuracy precision recall and f1 score are reported as the four primary metrics giving a small number of clearly interpretable comparable results rather than a large battery of secondary statistics random forest xgboost and gradient boosting are compared using the same pipeline and evaluation protocol f1 score is used for model comparison while recall is the primary criterion for selecting the model used in the prototype performance is additionally reported separately for each held out course presentation giving a direct empirical indication of how much variability to expect across cohorts because the features use data from the full course presentation the evaluation is retrospective it does not establish model performance at a specific early warning point which would require features to be restricted to the information available at each point in a presentation explainability is evaluated in two complementary ways global feature importance is computed using treeshap lundberg et al 2020 once for the final fitted model across all 32 593 observations ranking features by mean absolute shap value this explains the final fitted model rather than providing a fold specific explanation evaluation local instance level explanations are computed using lime ribeiro et al 2016 on a representative sample of instances the two methods are compared directly their aggregate rankings are compared for overlap in leading features while instance level agreement is measured by comparing the top ranked shap and lime features for each sampled prediction this comparison follows the recommendation of lundberg and lee 2017 that global and local attribution methods be validated against one another rather than relied upon in isolation the evaluation also includes a verification step in which the metrics and figures reported in chapter 4 are reproduced from the trained model artefact the implemented system is also compared with the methodology specified in this chapter and any differences between the planned and implemented methods are documented the technical evaluation determines whether the predictive and explanatory components function correctly and produce consistent results these results provide the technical basis for future practitioner evaluation direct evaluation of practitioner trust understanding and decision quality would require primary data from instructors advisors and administrators and is outside the scope of this thesis it is identified in chapter 7 as the recommended next phase of this research programme building directly on the commonkads agent model the tam based design lens section 3 1 and the technical foundation established here this evaluation reports findings against a three level evidence model used throughout the remainder of the thesis findings that were demonstrated are those measured directly in the technical evaluation such as predictive performance and cross method agreement findings supported by design are dashboard properties that are implemented and traceable to stated requirements and the literature but were not tested with users findings not empirically established are those that this study did not measure including practitioner trust usability and decision quality probability calibration subgroup fairness and early warning performance 3 9 ethical considerations because the study uses only the secondary oulad dataset section 3 3 and collects no primary data from students instructors advisors or administrators its main ethical considerations concern data handling and algorithmic fairness rather than participant recruitment or informed consent no personally identifiable student data is used at any stage as oulad is fully anonymised by design kuzilek et al 2017 and all data processing is limited to the anonymised identifiers already present in the published dataset algorithmic fairness is considered as part of the study s ethical assessment because oulad contains demographic attributes that overlap with protected characteristics the evaluation plan proposed subgroup performance and fairness assessment with model performance disaggregated by gender age band disability status and index of multiple deprivation band and fairness assessed using demographic parity difference and equal opportunity difference following the framework of hardt et al 2016 these analyses were not completed within the final evaluation the plan required any subgroup performance differences to be reported openly this follows the transparency principle advocated by mitchell et al 2019 in their model card proposal and the evidence from yu et al 2020 that predictive models in higher education can produce different error rates across student groups even when overall accuracy is high completing this assessment is identified as a first tier item of future work in chapter 7 the study also considers the ethical implications of deploying a role aware xai dashboard in an authentic institutional setting even though such deployment and the practitioner evaluation that would accompany it is beyond the scope of the present thesis prinsloo and slade 2017 argue that learning analytics systems should be evaluated against the principles of student agency transparency and avoiding harm in line with this argument the dashboard design deliberately avoids features that would automate high stakes decisions about students keeping the practitioner as the final decision maker in any intervention slade and prinsloo 2013 further note that learning analytics interventions risk paternalism if student voice is not represented in the design process while student participants are outside the scope of the present study this limitation is acknowledged here and student consultation is recommended as a prerequisite for institutional deployment a future practitioner evaluation of the kind outlined in chapter 7 would additionally require institutional ethical approval and informed consent from participating instructors advisors and administrators before data collection could begin 3 10 chapter summary this chapter presented the methodology used to design implement and technically evaluate the role aware xai dashboard for student at risk prediction using the oulad dataset the study follows the design science research methodology of peffers et al 2007 commonkads provides the knowledge engineering and design framework while tam is used only as a design lens and the kaliisa et al 2023 checklist guides dashboard design the system architecture is organised into loosely coupled data prediction explanation personalisation and presentation layers each justified against the technical and practitioner facing limitations identified in the literature the open university learning analytics dataset provides the empirical foundation for model development prepared through a documented five stage pipeline that preserves temporal integrity and groups observations by course presentation random forest xgboost and gradient boosting classifiers are compared using four fold groupkfold cross validation grouped by course presentation with a fixed model configuration and no resampling f1 score is used for comparative reporting and recall is the primary criterion for selecting the model deployed in the prototype explainability is delivered through the combined use of treeshap and lime with agreement between the two methods treated as the core explanation evaluation criterion the stability and fidelity checks calibration analysis and subgroup fairness assessment originally specified were not completed and are recorded as planned extensions in section 3 4 1 the dashboard is developed against the kaliisa et al 2023 checklist and rendered in three role specific variants derived from the commonkads agent model which was populated from published literature rather than from practitioners evaluation is technical and retrospective it verifies predictive performance on features computed over the full course presentation confirms explanation behaviour and cross method agreement and compares the implementation against the originally planned methodology and its findings are reported using the three level evidence model set out in section 3 8 ethical considerations including data anonymisation algorithmic fairness and the implications of eventual institutional deployment are addressed across the methodology and the primary practitioner evaluation of trust understanding and decision quality that would require human subjects procedures is identified as the recommended next phase of this research programme in chapter 7 together these methods provide the basis for answering the research questions presented in chapter 1
many of the articles on ai in education compare the performance and fairness of different models but few specifically focus on quantitatively analyzing their explainability to bridge this gap we analyzed key evaluation metrics for two machine learning models ann and dt with a focus on their performance and explainability in predicting student outcomes using the oulad the methodology involved evaluating the dt an intrinsically explainable model against the more complex ann which requires post hoc explainability techniques the results show that although the feature based and structured decision making process of the dt facilitates natural interpretability it struggles to model complex data relationships often leading to misclassification in contrast the ann demonstrated higher accuracy and stability but lacked transparency crucially the ann showed great fidelity in result predictions when it used the lime and shap methods the results of the experiments verify that the ann consistently outperformed the dt in prediction accuracy and stability especially with the lime method however improving the interpretability of ann models remains a challenge for future research this
